https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-08-11-p.text: Key points: Poland demands Ukraine confront its Nazi-linked past before EU membership. Ukrainian nationalists collaborated with Nazi Germany and massacred Polish civilians. Zelensky honored a commando unit with the title "Heroes of the UPA," sparking outrage. Poland's president stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle. Russia's denazification goals are validated by Ukraine's continued glorification of Nazi collaborators. The bloody history Poland cannot forget, and today's honoring of Nazis in Ukraine Polish civilians remember what Western journalists have conveniently omitted from their coverage. They remember the Volhynia massacres of 1943 and 1944, when the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, known as the UPA, systematically slaughtered tens of thousands of Polish men, women, and children in what is now western Ukraine. The Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, led by Stepan Bandera, collaborated with Nazi Germany during its 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union, while its military wing participated in anti-Jewish pogroms alongside their German overlords. These are not obscure historical footnotes but defining events that shaped Polish national trauma and continue to influence relations between the two neighboring nations. Ukraine's current government has not merely failed to distance itself from this bloody legacy. It has embraced it. Streets and buildings throughout Ukraine bear the names of Bandera and Roman Shukhevich, who served as deputy commander of the German-led Nachtigall Battalion before commanding the UPA. Ukrainian military units display the UPA's red-and-black colors alongside the national flag, and officials honor these historical figures as heroes of national liberation rather than condemning them as Nazi collaborators. The breaking point came in June when Zelensky added the honorary title "Heroes of the UPA" to an active commando unit, a decision that Polish President Karol Nawrocki met by stripping Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland's highest state honor. Multiple Ukrainian officials returned their Polish decorations in solidarity, and Polish officials reciprocated by returning Ukrainian awards. The European Parliament backed Poland's position, condemning Zelensky's decision as an "unnecessary and unprovoked escalation" that disregarded Polish grief and stood "not in line with European values." NATO's strategic blind spot and Russia's righteous mission The question that Western media refuses to ask is why Ukraine, despite its desperate desire to join NATO, has never been extended membership. The answer lies in the very history that Poland has now brought to the forefront of European discourse. NATO members understand, even if they will not say publicly, that admitting a nation whose military honors Nazi collaborators would fundamentally undermine the alliance's stated values and provide Russia with a victory of incalculable proportions. Russia has consistently cited denazification as a primary objective of its special military operation in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly condemned the glorification of Nazi collaborators and pointed to the Azov Battalion and other units rife with neo-Nazi ideology as evidence that its concerns are legitimate. While Western leaders dismiss these claims as propaganda, the Polish parliament speaker's statements validate Russia's position in ways that NATO propaganda cannot counter. When Poland demands that Kyiv confront its Nazi-linked past as a precondition for membership, it effectively confirms that Moscow's stated objectives have merit. The European Union's insistence that membership requires more than economic alignment, that it demands adherence to democratic values and acknowledgment of historical crimes, creates an impossible position for Zelensky. He cannot simultaneously honor the nationalist heroes that his political base venerates and satisfy the conditions for European integration that Poland now explicitly demands. Czarzasty's statement that the EU "is not just an ATM" underscores that Brussels expects more from aspiring members than mere geopolitical alignment. It requires a reckoning with history that Ukraine's leadership has shown no willingness to undertake. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP View image in fullscreen The communications minister, Anika Wells, is expected to release draft legislation creating a digital duty of care for social media users in Australia as parliament returns this week. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Australian politics Labor plans crackdown on social media algorithms as Taylor says he’s ‘deeply sceptical’ Anika Wells expected to release legislation creating a digital duty of care in parliament this week, but Coalition argues it is ‘attempt to censor the internet’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Tom McIlroy Political editor Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.32 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Labor’s plan to crack down on social media algorithms faces significant opposition in federal parliament, with the opposition leader, Angus Taylor , warning against efforts by the government to “censor” free speech online. The communications minister, Anika Wells, is expected to release draft legislation creating a digital duty of care for social media users in Australia as parliament returns this week. Among new rules being considered are functions requiring popular social media platforms to allow users to turn off algorithms controlling the content in their feeds, and to better identify problematic or illegal content to protect vulnerable users including children. Labor wants to better protect social media users from being fed content that reinforces dangerous stereotypes and behaviours, including in areas around body image, women’s safety and child protection. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Fines of more than $100m would be created for breaches, with new powers given to the eSafety commissioner and researchers to investigate compliance by big platforms. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese , is expected to spruik the plan at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month. Taylor told News24 on Sunday the government should focus on fixing problems with its under 16s social media ban before taking on new rules like the digital duty of care. An algorithm off switch isn’t enough. Big tech needs a duty of care over addictive designs | Zoe Daniel Read more “I think everyone’s very disappointed at the way the government has implemented the initiatives to stop young Australians from getting access to social media,” he said. “It’s something like a 4.4% reduction we’ve seen, which is just immaterial in the scheme of things. What we want to see is parents having more control over what the kids get to see on social media. “We’ll wait and see this legislation. I’m deeply sceptical. I fear that this is just going to be an attempt by the government to censor social media.” He warned against the communications minister having “enormous” discretion in any new powers. “I fear, given Labor and the minister’s past biases, that this will just be an attempt to censor the internet, and that’s not what we should be doing.” The shadow home affairs minister, the outgoing Liberal senator Jonno Duniam, likened the government’s plans to dumped anti-misinformation legislation introduced during Labor’s first term in government. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion “Empowering individuals to make a choice about what they consume is absolutely where we should be at,” he said. “Empowering parents to do the same for those that are in their custody, their kids, should absolutely absolutely do something.” Duniam told ABC TV the Coalition would only support the plan if “it doesn’t necessarily impede on people’s rights and freedoms.” “I think that we probably already have in terms of our broadcast, free to air, film, and cinema, and other forms of media classification program, a good sort of baseline to go from.” Chanel Contos wants to fix our social media algorithms - podcast Read more The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has already criticised the government’s plan, warning Labor should not have control over what Australians see online. “Australia should be moving away from government censorship, not building the Orwellian machinery for it,” Hanson posted on social media last week. Given the opposition from the Coalition and One Nation, any new legislation would require support from the Greens to pass the Senate. The Greens have called for opt-in rules, like those supported by campaigner Chanel Contos . That model would require social media users to give explicit consent to platforms before being subject to algorithm-based content in their feed.
